What a strange little chapter. I read most of it, and skimmed the rest. His overall conclusion, in my words, is that UBI disincentivizes work, which eliminates opportunities, therefore impoverishing receivers of UBI income, which would grow to 95% of the population.

He spends a lot of words to pin down "work" -- which mostly comes down to self-actualizing production of value -- culminating in the bullet points on p. 15, which are either redundant with any concise economic definition of "utility," or part of the "ontology of work" which requires that it fulfill a "social purpose." To me, feelings of purpose are sufficiently captured by economic utility or the previous requirement of an intent to a specific goal, but obviously his audience is not like me. The chapter finishes by detailing how this definition of "work" and what it provides people in wealth creation and satisfaction can not be achieved with leisure alone (p. 23). Since UBI grows leisure somewhat, then it enforces even more "leisure" on others by reducing opportunity to work. This is similar-sounding to me to the argument that prices will spiral out of control -- leisure will spiral out of control -- but I'm not sure how connected they are. Finally, he concludes that this lack of opportunity is in fact an enforced removal of agency, which prohibits self-actualization entirely. Thus the "feudalism" label.

It's an interesting argument. It could have been made in a much more economically-literate way, I'm sure. I wonder if the book goes on to anticipate arguments against his own. It really muddles the term "work" in order to satisfy requirements which his argument doesn't seem to require. It rests a lot on "a purpose greater than ourselves," separating "scarcity value," "utility value," and "aesthetic value" unnecessarily as if he is the judge of a consumer's economic-utility function; and mixing in personal agency with our "social role," all as if to head off an anti-capitalist argument (maybe his own) which doesn't require these compromises to defeat.

This is definitely a piece to keep bookmarked as UBI proponents become more numerous and powerful.
